title: New Scientist Story Ideas — Exercise — October 2026

studies.title: Being told you did worse than average makes you exercise harder — and feel worse about your body
studies.ns_score_reason: pre-registered experiment with a clean trade-off result, but a student lab sample and no follow-up beyond the session.
studies.the_study: In a pre-registered lab experiment, 120 participants did the same no-equipment workout twice. Between trials they were told their first performance was 30% below average, 30% above average, or given no feedback. Those told they were below average improved their objective performance and exertion far more than the other groups — but also showed the largest drops in body satisfaction and the largest rises in negative mood, with both effects strongest in people who identified most closely with the comparison group.
studies.why_it_matters: Social-comparison nudges are built into fitness apps, leaderboards and gym classes on the assumption that they are harmlessly motivating; this is the first direct evidence that the motivational boost and a body-image cost arrive together in the same session.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the leaderboard at the end of a spin class, or the app notification telling you you're in the bottom third this week. The surprise: the feedback works — and that's the problem. Call Olivia Davies and Tegan Cruwys at the Australian National University, whose social-identity framing explains why the sting is worst among people who care most about the group they're being ranked against.
studies.wider_angle: A consumer-tech feature on the ethics of behavioral nudges in fitness and wellness products — who audits a feature that raises engagement metrics while lowering mood? Fits a technology or business outlet covering app design and "dark patterns" in health.
studies.caveats: Single-center lab study; N=120 with 40 per condition; outcomes measured immediately, so no evidence on whether either the performance gain or the body-image hit persists; student population may not generalize to older or clinical groups.

studies.title: Three minutes a day beats two half-hour workouts a week
studies.ns_score_reason: randomized, directly testable by any reader, but short and reliant on self-tracked activity.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: 142 participants were randomized to a "micro goal" (3 minutes of exercise every day plus two 20-minute sessions a week) or a standard goal (two 30-minute sessions a week) and tracked their exercise, enjoyment and ease of adherence for three weeks. The micro goal group accumulated significantly more total exercise time, and the effect was mediated by how easy people found it to stick to the goal.
studies.why_it_matters: The micro-habit idea is everywhere in self-help but barely tested; this is a randomized test showing the mechanism is not motivation or enjoyment but sheer ease of compliance — which has implications for how public health guidance is worded.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the arithmetic that shouldn't work — a goal of three minutes a day ends up producing *more* exercise in total than a goal built around proper workouts. Open on someone who has abandoned a gym membership twice. Worth calling Katy Tapper's group at City St George's, University of London, who ran the trial and can speak to whether the gain survives beyond three weeks.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on the evidence base — or lack of one — behind the habit-formation industry: atomic habits, streaks, two-minute rules. Which of these popular claims have ever been randomized? Good fit for a long-read in a general-interest magazine or a behavioral-science podcast.
studies.caveats: Self-reported daily exercise duration; three-week follow-up only, so no evidence on durable habit formation; no objective activity measurement; participants knew which condition they were in.

studies.title: We judge people's health habits as moral failings only when we think they hurt someone else
studies.ns_score_reason: five studies, experimental manipulation and a clean theoretical result; limited by largely online samples.
studies.the_study: Across five studies with 2,055 participants, researchers tested why people treat health behaviors — smoking, eating well, exercising — as moral rather than merely practical. Perceived *interpersonal* harm, the sense that your poor health hurts other people, consistently predicted moralization, and experimentally increasing a behavior's apparent interpersonal harmfulness caused participants to moralize it. Disgust, a leading rival explanation, had no unique effect.
studies.why_it_matters: It offers a testable account of why the gym-going, clean-eating virtue narrative has the grip it does, and why health campaigns framed around burdening others can tip into stigma.
studies.pitch_angle: Why does skipping the gym feel like a minor sin? Open on the moral vocabulary people use about exercise — "being good", "earning" a dessert — and the finding that it tracks perceived harm to others, not disgust. Call Kurt Gray (Ohio State) or Sophie Pratt and A. Janet Tomiyama (UCLA); Tomiyama's weight-stigma work gives the piece its sharpest edge.
studies.wider_angle: A public-health policy story: campaigns that emphasize the cost of unhealthy behavior to families, the health service or society are, on this evidence, directly manufacturing moral condemnation. Suited to a health-policy or current-affairs outlet.
studies.caveats: Mostly online samples of uncertain demographic breadth; vignette-based manipulations measure judgments, not real-world behavior toward stigmatized people; cross-cultural generalizability untested.

studies.title: Ten minutes of "exercise snacks" a day lowers office workers' blood pressure and stress
studies.ns_score_reason: a real 12-week workplace RCT with objective blood-pressure outcomes, but only 52 participants and no blinding.
studies.the_study: 52 office workers were randomized to 12 weeks of "Exercise-Snacks" — three to six daily bouts of stair climbing, brisk walking, squats, push-ups or stretching lasting 1–3 minutes each, around 10 minutes a day in total — or to no intervention. By week 12 the intervention group's systolic blood pressure had fallen 4.6 mmHg and diastolic 2.4 mmHg, with perceived stress down 2.5 points on the PSS-10. BMI did not change.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the psychological and cardiovascular benefits of breaking up sedentary work do not require a lunchtime workout or any weight loss — a genuinely low-friction target for employers, though one small trial is not a basis for policy.
studies.pitch_angle: Pair this with the micro-goals trial above as evidence that the smallest credible dose of exercise is doing real work. Open on the stairwell at 3 p.m. The hook: the blood-pressure drop arrived with no change in body weight at all, which undercuts the assumption that exercise benefits run through the scales. Contact Kai Liu at Korea University.
studies.wider_angle: An occupational-health piece on whether the hybrid-work era has quietly made the standing-desk debate obsolete — the intervention that actually interrupts sitting is movement, not furniture. Fits a business or workplace-focused outlet.
studies.caveats: Small N (52) and single-site; no attention-control group, so expectancy effects cannot be excluded; perceived stress is self-reported; adherence monitoring not described in the abstract; short follow-up with no post-intervention measurement.

studies.title: For older adults, being shown how to exercise matters more for mood than how much they exercise
studies.ns_score_reason: large national longitudinal sample, but observational and self-reported throughout.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Using three waves of the China Longitudinal Aging Social Survey (2020–2023), researchers analyzed 5,643 adults aged 60–75. Both physical activity volume and receiving exercise guidance were associated with fewer depressive symptoms, but the association for sheer activity volume was inconsistent across subgroups, while guidance held up more robustly — and was more strongly conditioned on how often people used the internet and how digitally capable they felt.
studies.why_it_matters: It hints that the mood benefit older people get from exercise may depend less on minutes accumulated than on whether anyone is showing them what to do — and that digital exclusion may be quietly gating access to that guidance.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is the ranking: volume of activity was the shakier predictor, guidance the sturdier one. Open on a rural respondent with no smartphone and no local class. Call the Soochow University team; worth pressing them on whether "guidance" is a proxy for social contact rather than instruction.
studies.wider_angle: A demographics and digital-divide story — as exercise advice migrates to apps and video, who is left out, and what does that cost in later-life mental health? Fits an aging, technology or international-development outlet.
studies.caveats: Observational — cannot establish causation; physical activity, exercise guidance, digital proficiency and depressive symptoms all self-reported; Chinese young-old population may not generalize; residual confounding by health status and social contact is likely.

studies.title: Fitness Instagram is linked to more exercise — but only in people who don't see themselves as exercisers
studies.ns_score_reason: an interesting moderation result readers will recognize, but cross-sectional and self-reported.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: In a cross-sectional survey of emerging adults, higher fitness-related Instagram use was associated with more moderate-to-vigorous and total physical activity. But the association split by self-concept: among people with an "exercise self-schema" — those who already see being an exerciser as central to who they are — fitness-related Instagram use showed no relationship with activity at all. The positive association was carried entirely by people without that self-image.
studies.why_it_matters: It complicates the standard worry that fitness content mainly preaches to the converted or demoralizes everyone else, suggesting instead that its only measurable correlate with activity sits in the group least likely to be targeted by it.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on someone who has never thought of themselves as "sporty" doom-scrolling gym reels. The hook: the people for whom fitness content appears to do nothing are the committed exercisers. Call Sarah Grace and Daheia Barr-Anderson at the University of Minnesota, and ask the obvious causal question out loud — does the feed drive the activity, or the reverse?
studies.wider_angle: A media-studies feature on how fitness influencer content is actually consumed, and whether platforms could be designed to reach non-identifying exercisers. Suited to a digital-culture or sports-media outlet.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional — direction of the association is indeterminate, and reverse causation is highly plausible; self-reported physical activity and Instagram use; sample limited to emerging adults; no measure of content type.

studies.title: Eating disorder clinicians say they lack any guidance on the compulsive exercise they treat daily
studies.ns_score_reason: a stark, quotable treatment-gap finding, but a modest survey from one country.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: A cross-sectional survey of 102 clinicians working in Swedish eating disorder services found that although most regard maladaptive exercise as a symptom that worsens outcomes, few had received formal training and only moderate confidence in managing it. Assessment was routine but structured intervention was rare; just 42% had access to any clinic-level practice or informal protocol, while 84% said national guidance was needed.
studies.why_it_matters: Compulsive exercise is one of the most common and most dangerous features of restrictive eating disorders, and this suggests it is being routinely detected and then left untreated for want of any agreed method.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the 42% figure. Open on a clinician who records a patient's compulsive running at intake and then has nothing in the protocol to do about it. Call Elin Monell at Karolinska Institutet or Elisabeth Forsén Mantilla at the Swedish School of Sport and Health Sciences; the companion Italian work on acute "urges to move" (PMID 42490250) gives the piece a second limb.
studies.wider_angle: A health-services investigation into how exercise is handled inside eating disorder treatment across the UK or US — including whether patients are told to stop entirely, which clinicians increasingly question. Fits a health-reporting outlet or a specialist psychiatry publication.
studies.caveats: Small survey (N=102), single country, self-reported knowledge and practice; responders may be those most interested in the topic; no patient outcomes measured.

studies.title: "Realistic" postpartum workout images still leave new mothers feeling worse about their bodies
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely unexpected null-plus-backfire, but tiny and exploratory.
studies.the_study: Researchers created imagery depicting safe, appropriate postpartum exercise — deliberately "realistic" rather than aspirational — and showed it to 33 women within 12 months of giving birth, with 21 followed up in interviews. Women reported body dissatisfaction *after* viewing the imagery, and asked for imagery that was more realistic still. Body dissatisfaction and activity levels did not differ between women who had and had not retained weight.
studies.why_it_matters: The standard fix for harmful fitness imagery — make it more representative — did not work as intended here, suggesting the problem for postpartum women may be the act of being shown an exercising body at all rather than which body is shown.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the "MomBod" of the study's title and the gap between what new mothers say they want to see and how they feel once they see it. The hook is the backfire against the obvious remedy. Call Iris Lesser at the University of the Fraser Valley, and ask what imagery, if any, cleared the bar.
studies.wider_angle: A reported feature on the postpartum fitness industry — six-week "bounce-back" programs, pelvic-floor neglect, and who actually supplies new mothers with exercise advice. Fits a parenting or women's-health outlet.
studies.caveats: Very small N (33 quantitative, 21 interviews); no control imagery condition; cross-sectional exposure with no follow-up; self-selected Canadian sample; qualitative findings not generalizable.

studies.title: Replaying a relaxation exercise to sleeping nightmare sufferers changes their sleep spindles — but not their nightmares
studies.ns_score_reason: a well-designed, blinded, crossover null that deflates a fashionable idea; limited by N=25 and two lab nights.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Twenty-five people experiencing at least one nightmare a week practiced a deep-breathing relaxation exercise for a week while paired with a distinctive odor. In a randomized, blinded crossover design, that odor or a control odor was then wafted at them across two laboratory nights. The reactivation did not reduce the high-frequency beta or gamma EEG activity thought to index cortical hyperarousal, and nightmare symptoms were unchanged — though it did unexpectedly reduce sleep spindle count and density.
studies.why_it_matters: Targeted memory reactivation during sleep has been widely reported as a way to strengthen learning and soften emotional memories; this is a careful test in a clinical population where it simply did not do what the model predicted.
studies.pitch_angle: Scent-cued learning during sleep is one of the most seductive findings in sleep science. Open on the lab, the odor dispenser and a volunteer who still woke from a nightmare. Lead with the honest negative result and the orphan finding — fewer spindles — that nobody can yet explain. Call Ines Wilhelm's group at the University of Luebeck.
studies.wider_angle: A broader feature on the replication record of sleep-based interventions, from targeted memory reactivation to acoustic slow-wave stimulation to sleep-learning apps: which effects survive blinding? Fits a science long-read or a neuroscience-focused outlet.
studies.caveats: Small N (25), predominantly young women; only two laboratory nights of reactivation, which the authors themselves flag as likely insufficient; nightmare symptoms self-reported; single-center.

studies.title: Teaching exercise through "feel it" cues beats instruction by demonstration on fitness and movement quality
studies.ns_score_reason: a 16-week randomized trial with objective kinematics, but a narrow sample and a loosely defined intervention.
studies.the_study: 63 female university students aged 18–25 were randomized to 32 sessions over 16 weeks of either conventional aerobics instruction or embodied cognition-based training emphasizing exploratory learning and sensorimotor awareness. Both improved on every fitness measure, but the embodied group gained significantly more in trunk and abdominal endurance, upper-body strength, agility and overall performance, and showed better joint kinematics — notably greater ankle range of motion and reduced knee flexion.
studies.why_it_matters: It is an unusually long randomized test of the claim that how an instructor directs attention — to internal sensation rather than to copying a model — changes what the body physically learns.
studies.pitch_angle: The gym-class question nobody tests: does it matter whether the instructor says "watch me" or "notice what your ankle is doing"? Open on 16 weeks of identical aerobics routines taught two ways, with video motion capture to settle it. Call Maryam Ghorbani and Rasoul Yaali at Kharazmi University, and press on how the instruction scripts actually differed.
studies.wider_angle: A sports-science feature on the long-running internal-versus-external focus of attention debate in motor learning, and what coaches of everyone from rehab patients to elite athletes currently do with it. Fits a sports or physiotherapy specialist outlet.
studies.caveats: Young female university students only — unlikely to generalize; single-center; instructors not blinded and likely differed in enthusiasm as well as method; kinematics extracted from 2D video software; no retention test after training ended.

studies.title: Prescribing exercise for pleasure gets people back to the gym — but not via the motivations theory predicts
studies.journal: Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuine theoretical puzzle, but a small ancillary analysis with a two-week intervention.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: 46 insufficiently active adults (mean age 32) were randomized to three supervised gym sessions over two weeks following either standard guideline-based prescription or a pleasure-oriented version tailored to intensity preference, self-selected intensity and repeated affective monitoring. Both groups improved on intention, habit, perceived choice, competence, intrinsic motivation and vitality — with no significant difference between them, implying the parent trial's increase in exercise frequency ran through some other, unidentified mechanism.
studies.why_it_matters: Hedonic approaches to exercise prescription are a fast-growing idea in behavior change; this says the effect may be real while the textbook explanation for it is wrong.
studies.pitch_angle: An honest negative mechanism paper: making exercise feel nicer got people exercising more, but none of the motivational constructs it was supposed to work through moved. Open on a first-time gym user being asked, mid-set, how they feel. Call Diogo Teixeira at Lusófona University.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on the quiet crisis in behavior-change theory — interventions that work while their mediators refuse to budge, across diet, smoking and exercise research. Fits a specialist psychology or research-methods publication.
studies.caveats: Small N (46); ancillary secondary analysis of a larger trial and not powered for these outcomes; two-week intervention with three sessions; all mediators self-reported; null results from an underpowered design do not rule out real effects.

studies.title: Team sport, solo spinning or karate — the mood lift after exercise looks much the same
studies.ns_score_reason: a useful real-world time-course of post-exercise mood, but the headline comparison is explicitly underpowered and the authors say so.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: 60 amateur athletes in three habitual training groups — cheerleading (interactive), spinning (coactive) and karate (hybrid) — had affect measured before, 15 minutes after and 60 minutes after a session. Positive affect rose and negative affect fell after exercise in all three, with arousal dropping below baseline an hour later while felt valence stayed elevated. No significant differences by sport type emerged, but the authors are unusually candid that the study could only detect large effects and that equivalence tests failed for all 24 contrasts.
studies.why_it_matters: The practical finding is about timing rather than type: the pleasant feeling outlasts the physiological arousal by at least an hour, which is a tidy, checkable claim about what exercise actually does to mood.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the hour after a workout — arousal already below where you started, but mood still lifted. Treat the sport-type comparison as the non-story the authors themselves say it is. Call Attila Szabo at ELTE, whose transparency about power and equivalence makes him a good interviewee on how null results should be reported.
studies.wider_angle: A methods-focused piece for a research or academic-publishing outlet on authors who refuse to launder an underpowered null as "no difference" — this abstract is a model of the genre.
studies.caveats: Small N (60) and non-randomized, with groups differing in age, sex, experience and session intensity; predominantly female sample with menstrual-cycle phase unrecorded; self-reported affect; explicitly underpowered for the main between-group comparison.

studies.title: Confidence in runners builds in one direction: believing in yourself shapes what you think others think of you
studies.journal: Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology
studies.ns_score_reason: a well-powered longitudinal design with a clear directional result, but a narrow psychological construct that is hard to make vivid.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: 350 runners completed surveys at three points over two months, analyzed with a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model — a design that separates within-person change from stable between-person differences. Self-efficacy at Time 1 predicted relation-inferred self-efficacy (your belief about how capable others think you are) at Time 2, and indirectly at Time 3. The reverse path did not hold, and social identification with the running group neither predicted nor followed from efficacy beliefs despite correlating with them at every time point.
studies.why_it_matters: It is the first longitudinal evidence on the direction of this loop, and it suggests the common coaching intuition that group belonging builds confidence may be a within-moment correlation rather than a process that unfolds over weeks.
studies.pitch_angle: The counterintuitive bit is what *didn't* move — feeling part of the running club went along with confidence but never preceded it. Open on a Parkrun. Call Samuel Stephen at the University of Calgary or Pete Coffee at Heriot-Watt, and ask whether two months is long enough for identity effects to show.
studies.wider_angle: A methods and sports-psychology piece on what happens when cross-lagged panel models are rerun with random intercepts — a quiet statistical correction that has been deflating a lot of previously confident directional claims across psychology. Fits a specialist psychology outlet.
studies.caveats: All self-reported; observational, so the cross-lagged path is suggestive rather than causal; two-month window may be too short; runners who volunteer for three surveys are a self-selected group; no behavioral or performance outcome.

studies.title: Most people with hard-to-treat epilepsy or dissociative seizures do no exercise at all
studies.ns_score_reason: a striking inactivity statistic in a rarely measured group, but the paper is primarily instrument development.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Researchers built a seizure-specific physical activity questionnaire (QESA) and short exercise and perceived-fitness scales, then applied them to 240 inpatients — 146 with epilepsy, 94 with functional/dissociative seizures with or without epilepsy — most of whom were not seizure-free and two-thirds of whom had psychiatric comorbidities. Physical activity was very low: 60% reported none at work and 41% none in leisure time. Strikingly, people with epilepsy exercised *less* than those with functional/dissociative seizures (57.2% versus 42.6% reporting no exercise).
studies.why_it_matters: Exercise is one of the few interventions with evidence across both seizure control and the depression that so often accompanies it, yet this population appears almost entirely sedentary — and the within-group difference hints that fear of seizures, not physical incapacity, may be doing the work.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on a patient who stopped swimming, then stopped cycling, then stopped walking far from home. The hook is that the group whose seizures are not epileptic in origin were the *more* active ones — suggesting the barrier is as much perceived risk and medical caution as pathology. Call Anne Hagemann at the Bethel Epilepsy Center.
studies.wider_angle: A disability and health-inequality story about how risk-averse medical advice can produce a second, chronic health problem — sedentary behavior — in people already managing a neurological condition. Fits a health-reporting or disability-focused outlet.
studies.caveats: Single-center inpatient sample, likely skewed toward severe and refractory cases; all activity self-reported via a newly developed instrument with only fair-to-good retest reliability (ICC 0.54–0.75); cross-sectional baseline data; no comparison with the general population.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- *Volume is the wrong unit.* The previous digest's dose ceiling for mind-body exercise in cancer patients (PMID 42412001) and the non-monotonic activity–suicidal-ideation curve in 214,218 Korean teenagers (PMID 42605073) are now joined by three studies pushing the same way from the low end: "Three minutes a day beats two half-hour workouts a week" (PMID 42704303), "Ten minutes of 'exercise snacks' a day lowers office workers' blood pressure and stress" (PMID 42810116), and "For older adults, being shown how to exercise matters more for mood than how much they exercise" (PMID 42807680), in which activity volume was the shakier predictor of depressive symptoms and received guidance the sturdier one.
- *Nulls published honestly by the people who had most to lose.* Last run's self-replication failure on exercise and retrieval-induced forgetting (PMID 42579016), the overturning of dynamic-norm messaging (PMID 42615122) and the interoception null (PMID 42526739) have close company here: the blinded crossover showing scent-cued relaxation reactivation does nothing for nightmares (PMID 42714131), the pleasure-prescription trial whose mediators refused to move (PMID 42772728), and an affect study whose authors state outright that equivalence tests failed for all 24 contrasts (PMID 42801814).
- *Exercise as a clinical blind spot.* The ISBD position statement conceding how thin the bipolar evidence base is (PMID 42545207) now has two concrete analogues: Swedish eating disorder clinicians who detect compulsive exercise but have no protocol for it (PMID 41982074), and the finding that most inpatients with refractory epilepsy or dissociative seizures do no exercise at all (PMID 42700754).

**Advances**
- Workplace exercise moves from perk to protocol: the previous digest's ClassPass trial in psychiatry residents shifted anxiety but not burnout (PMID 42362858); the new 12-week exercise-snacks RCT (PMID 42810116) delivers objective blood-pressure falls with no weight change, shifting the question from what employers buy to how the working day is broken up.
- The fitness-technology thread deepens. Previously it was readiness scores being deliberately overridden (PMID 42034345) and momentary lapse triggers (PMID 40415394); now it is who the technology reaches and at what cost — fitness Instagram correlating with activity only in people without an exercise self-schema (PMID 42803216), digital proficiency gating access to exercise guidance in older Chinese adults (PMID 42807680), and leaderboard-style social comparison raising effort while lowering body satisfaction (PMID 42805545).

**Counterpoints**
- The social-ingredient story gets trimmed. The 28-year Norwegian cohort suggested health behaviors buy company and reduce later loneliness (PMID 42544718); this batch finds social identification with a running group never preceded self-efficacy over two months (PMID 42722364), and no difference in post-exercise mood between interactive, coactive and hybrid sports (PMID 42801814) — though that comparison is explicitly underpowered.
- Previously, psychological nudges mostly underperformed (PMID 42615122, PMID 42520720). The new social-comparison experiment (PMID 42805545) shows one that works on objective performance — the catch is the simultaneous body-image hit, which relocates the problem from efficacy to ethics.

**New themes**
- Moralization: why health behaviors are judged as virtue or sin tracks perceived harm to other people, not disgust (PMID 41185114) — no antecedent in the previous digest.
- Instruction quality as an outcome variable: 16 weeks of identical aerobics taught with internal-sensation cues beat demonstration-based teaching on strength, agility and joint kinematics (PMID 42804848), pairing with the older-adult guidance finding (PMID 42807680).
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Several studies in this batch converge on the psychological packaging of exercise — the feedback, imagery and moral framing wrapped around it — and find that the packaging carries a measurable cost that nobody is auditing. Being told you performed below average improved objective effort while producing the largest drop in body satisfaction in the same session (PMID 42805545); deliberately "realistic" postpartum workout imagery still left new mothers feeling worse about their bodies (PMID 41724692); health behaviors get moralized specifically when they look harmful to other people, which is exactly how campaigns are framed (PMID 41185114); fitness Instagram correlates with activity only among people who don't already see themselves as exercisers (PMID 42803216) — and at the clinical end, eating disorder clinicians say they routinely assess compulsive exercise and then have nothing to do about it, with only 42% having access to any protocol (PMID 41982074).

**Why pitch this now:** Social comparison is now a default design feature of fitness apps, gym classes and workplace wellness programs, and public health messaging increasingly leans on the burden-to-others frame — both at the moment when the first direct evidence arrives that the motivational gain and the body-image cost are the same event, and when the clinicians who treat the downstream casualties say they have no agreed method.

**Angle:** A reported feature on the unmeasured side-effects of exercise motivation — tracing one design decision (the leaderboard, the "realistic" fitness photo, the "don't burden the NHS" campaign line) from the lab experiment through the app to the eating disorder clinic that has no protocol for what arrives. For general readers who use a fitness app, plus the product and public-health people who build these features.

**Potential headlines:**
- The leaderboard works, and that is the problem
- Making fitness pictures more realistic made new mothers feel worse
- Every app that ranks you against other people is running an experiment on your body image

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Mind** — the core experiment is a clean pre-registered trade-off result, and the section already carries body-image and behavior-change psychology for a readership that uses these apps.
- **Wired** — the dark-patterns framing is squarely theirs: a feature that raises engagement metrics while depressing mood is a product-design story as much as a psychology one.
- **The Guardian science desk** — strong existing coverage of eating disorders, postpartum health and fitness culture; the untreated compulsive-exercise gap gives the piece a UK-relevant services hook.
- **BBC Future** — suits the longer explanatory treatment of why moralized health messaging tips into stigma, with the five-study moralization paper as the spine.

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind digest, run date 2026-10-05

---

### Study 1: Being told you did worse than average makes you exercise harder — and feel worse about your body
**PMID:** 42805545 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Moderation attributed to the wrong outcomes** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "but also showed the largest drops in body satisfaction and the largest rises in negative mood, with both effects strongest in people who identified most closely with the comparison group."
- **Abstract says:** "Moderation analyses indicated that the effects of the norm feedback on performance (F(2, 114) = 4.55, p = .13) and body satisfaction (F(2, 114) = 7.19, p = .001) were moderated by social identification such that its effects were stronger among those who strongly identified with the norm reference group."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports moderation tests for *performance* and *body satisfaction* — not negative mood. The digest transfers the moderation to negative mood, an outcome for which no moderation result is reported. Separately, the performance moderation is printed as p = .13, i.e. non-significant as reported, so only the body-satisfaction moderation is clearly supported.
- **Suggested fix:** "but also showed the largest drops in body satisfaction and the largest rises in negative mood, with the body-satisfaction effect strongest in people who identified most closely with the comparison group."

Note: the pitch angle ("the sting is worst among people who care most about the group") should be narrowed to body satisfaction for the same reason. NS fit of 7/10 is defensible — pre-registered, randomized, with an objective performance outcome.

---

### Study 2: Three minutes a day beats two half-hour workouts a week
**PMID:** 42704303 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

**Issue A. Headline and pitch omit the two 20-minute sessions in the micro-goal condition** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Three minutes a day beats two half-hour workouts a week" / "a goal of three minutes a day ends up producing *more* exercise in total than a goal built around proper workouts"
- **Abstract says:** "Participants (n = 142) were randomly assigned to a micro goal group (3 min daily plus two 20-minute sessions weekly) or a standard goal group (two 30-minute sessions weekly)."
- **Problem:** The micro-goal condition was *not* three minutes a day instead of longer workouts — it included two 20-minute sessions a week as well, so the two prescribed weekly totals were near-identical (≈61 vs 60 minutes). A reader of the headline will take away that three minutes a day alone outperformed half-hour sessions, which the study did not test.
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "Adding a three-minute daily goal to weekly workouts gets people exercising more." Body: "a goal that added three daily minutes to two shorter weekly sessions produced more total exercise than two 30-minute sessions, despite near-identical prescribed weekly totals."

**Issue B. "Motivation" was not tested as a mechanism** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "this is a randomized test showing the mechanism is not motivation or enjoyment but sheer ease of compliance"
- **Abstract says:** "Participants tracked their daily exercise duration, enjoyment, and ease of adherence over 3 wk. The micro goal group exercised significantly more time overall than the standard goal group, with ease of adherence mediating this effect."
- **Problem:** Enjoyment was measured; motivation was not, per the abstract. The abstract also does not report a failed mediation test for enjoyment, only a successful one for ease of adherence.
- **Suggested fix:** "a randomized test in which the effect was mediated by ease of adherence rather than by enjoyment."

**Issue C. NS fit score** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 — randomized, directly testable by any reader, but short and reliant on self-tracked activity."
- **Problem:** A three-week trial with entirely self-tracked exercise duration, unblinded participants, and no objective activity measure is thin ground for a 7. The score note itself concedes both weaknesses.
- **Suggested fix:** Score 6/10.

### Study 3: We judge people's health habits as moral failings only when we think they hurt someone else
**PMID:** 41185114 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Wider angle conflates collective harm with interpersonal harm** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "campaigns that emphasize the cost of unhealthy behavior to families, the health service or society are, on this evidence, directly manufacturing moral condemnation."
- **Abstract says:** "We identified three types of harm-personal, interpersonal, and collective... Perceived interpersonal harm reliably predicted moralizations of health."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports that *interpersonal* harm was the reliable predictor and the manipulated variable. Collective harm (cost to the health service or society) is a separate construct that the abstract does not report as predictive. The pitch extends the finding to a harm type the study distinguished and did not support.
- **Suggested fix:** "campaigns that emphasize the cost of unhealthy behaviour to family and close others are, on this evidence, likely to amplify moral condemnation — though the study found the effect for interpersonal, not collective, harm."

**Issue B. Sample composition** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "limited by largely online samples" / "Mostly online samples of uncertain demographic breadth"
- **Abstract says:** Nothing about recruitment platform or sample composition.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only. Reasonable as a hedge, but it should not be stated as fact.
- **Suggested fix:** "Sample recruitment and demographics are not described in the abstract and should be checked against the full text."

NS fit 7/10 is defensible: five studies, N = 2,055, with experimental manipulation in two of them.

### Study 4: Ten minutes of "exercise snacks" a day lowers office workers' blood pressure and stress
**PMID:** 42810116 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Within-group changes presented as controlled intervention effects** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "By week 12 the intervention group's systolic blood pressure had fallen 4.6 mmHg and diastolic 2.4 mmHg, with perceived stress down 2.5 points on the PSS-10."
- **Abstract says:** "At week 6, significant group × time interactions emerged for SBP and PSS-10 but not for DBP or BMI. By week 12, SBP, DBP, and PSS-10 in the intervention group decreased from baseline by 4.6 mmHg... 2.4 mmHg... and 2.5 points..."
- **Problem:** The three numbers are within-group changes from baseline, not between-group differences. The only group × time interactions the abstract reports are at week 6, and DBP was *not* significant there. The digest's framing (and the headline verb "lowers") implies all three are controlled effects; the DBP claim in particular is not supported by a reported interaction.
- **Suggested fix:** "At week 6 the intervention outperformed the control on systolic blood pressure and perceived stress but not diastolic pressure or BMI. By week 12 the intervention group's own readings were down 4.6 mmHg systolic, 2.4 mmHg diastolic and 2.5 points on the PSS-10 from baseline; BMI did not change."

**Issue B. Control condition described as "no intervention"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "or to no intervention"
- **Abstract says:** "assigning office workers to an Exercise-Snack intervention (n = 25) or control (n = 27)."
- **Problem:** The abstract does not describe what the control group received. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "or to a control condition (not described in the abstract)."

Group sizes (25 + 27 = 52) and BMI null are reported correctly. NS fit 6/10 is defensible.

### Study 5: For older adults, being shown how to exercise matters more for mood than how much they exercise
**PMID:** 42807680 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline asserts a causal ranking from observational data** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "For older adults, being shown how to exercise matters more for mood than how much they exercise"
- **Abstract says:** "PAV and EG were associated with lower depressive symptom scores in the full sample, although the association for PAV was less consistent across subgroup and moderation models."
- **Problem:** "Matters more for mood" reads as a causal effect on a causal comparison. The study is a GEE analysis of self-reported survey data; the finding is that one association was more *consistent* across models, which is not the same as one factor mattering more. The body text and caveats hedge properly, but the headline does not.
- **Suggested fix:** "For older adults, exercise guidance is a more consistent correlate of mood than how much they exercise"

**Issue B. Number of waves** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Using three waves of the China Longitudinal Aging Social Survey (2020–2023)"
- **Abstract says:** "Data were drawn from the 2020 to 2023 waves of the China Longitudinal Aging Social Survey (CLASS)."
- **Problem:** The abstract does not state how many waves this spans. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Using the 2020–2023 waves of the China Longitudinal Aging Social Survey."

N (5,643), age band (60–75) and the digital-engagement moderation are reported accurately. NS fit 6/10 is defensible.

### Study 6: Fitness Instagram is linked to more exercise — but only in people who don't see themselves as exercisers
**PMID:** 42803216 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Author first name** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Call Sarah Grace and Daheia Barr-Anderson at the University of Minnesota"
- **Abstract says:** "Grace SM(1)... Barr-Anderson DJ(1). University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA."
- **Problem:** The first author's given name is not in the abstract (initials S.M.). Unverifiable from abstract only — worth confirming before the pitch goes out.

Everything else checks out: the β values are correctly characterized in direction, the self-schema moderation is correctly described (no association among those with an exercise self-schema; positive association among those without), and the cross-sectional caveat and reverse-causation warning are appropriately prominent. ### Study 7: Eating disorder clinicians say they lack any guidance on the compulsive exercise they treat daily
**PMID:** 41982074 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline overstates the absence of guidance and invents a treatment frequency** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Eating disorder clinicians say they lack any guidance on the compulsive exercise they treat daily"
- **Abstract says:** "Only 42% reported access to clinic-level practices/informal protocols, while 84% expressed a need for national guidance."
- **Problem:** Two problems. First, 42% *did* report access to clinic-level practice or protocol, so "lack any guidance" is wrong for a substantial minority; what is absent is *national* guidance. Second, "they treat daily" is not measured anywhere in the abstract — assessment was common, but treatment frequency was not quantified.
- **Suggested fix:** "Most eating disorder clinicians say they have no agreed protocol for the compulsive exercise they routinely assess"

**Issue B. Escalated risk language** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Compulsive exercise is one of the most common and most dangerous features of restrictive eating disorders"
- **Abstract says:** "Maladaptive exercise is a common and serious symptom in eating disorders (EDs), yet often poorly addressed in treatment."
- **Problem:** "One of the most dangerous" and the narrowing to "restrictive" eating disorders both go beyond "a common and serious symptom in eating disorders."
- **Suggested fix:** "Maladaptive exercise is a common and serious symptom in eating disorders"

**Issue C. Companion study reference** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the companion Italian work on acute 'urges to move' (PMID 42490250) gives the piece a second limb."
- **Problem:** No abstract supplied for PMID 42490250. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** Verify the second paper's content and country before including it in the pitch.

N (102), the 84% figure, the "assessment common / structured intervention rare" contrast and the Karolinska / Swedish School of Sport and Health Sciences affiliations are all correct. NS fit 5/10 is appropriate.

### Study 8: "Realistic" postpartum workout images still leave new mothers feeling worse about their bodies
**PMID:** 41724692 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Backfire" framing implies a worsening the design cannot show** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** Counterintuitive... a genuinely unexpected null-plus-backfire" / "The hook is the backfire against the obvious remedy." / Headline: "still leave new mothers feeling worse about their bodies"
- **Abstract says:** "Findings suggest women experience body dissatisfaction after viewing imagery and desire 'realistic' PA imagery."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports that women *experienced* body dissatisfaction after viewing the imagery — it reports no pre-exposure baseline, no control imagery and no statistical test of change. "Leave them feeling worse" and "backfire" both assert that the imagery made things worse, which this design cannot establish. The caveats flag the absent control condition, but the headline and pitch contradict that caveat rather than respecting it. The only reported null (no difference between weight-retention and weight-loss groups) concerns a different comparison entirely.
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "New mothers still report body dissatisfaction after viewing 'realistic' postpartum exercise imagery." Pitch: "The hook is that women shown deliberately realistic imagery still reported dissatisfaction afterwards — and asked for imagery more realistic still."

N (33 questionnaires, 21 interviews), the <12 months postpartum window, the weight-retention null and the Fraser Valley affiliation are all accurate. NS fit 5/10 is appropriate for an exploratory mixed-methods study.

### Study 9: Replaying a relaxation exercise to sleeping nightmare sufferers changes their sleep spindles — but not their nightmares
**PMID:** 42714131 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Failed replication" is the wrong novelty label** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** Failed replication"
- **Abstract says:** "its precise role remains insufficiently understood because experimental approaches to manipulate hyperarousal during sleep are limited. In the present study, we investigated whether..."
- **Problem:** This is a first experimental test of odour-cued reactivation of a relaxation exercise in frequent nightmare sufferers, not an attempt to reproduce a prior study. The body text ("this is a careful test in a clinical population") describes it correctly; the label does not.
- **Suggested fix:** "**Novelty:** Null result / first test"

Everything else is accurate: N = 25, ≥1 nightmare a week, one-week training, randomized blinded crossover, two lab nights, no beta/gamma effect, nightmare symptoms unchanged, unexpected reduction in spindle count and density, Wilhelm at University of Luebeck. The "authors flag longer reactivation periods" caveat matches the abstract. NS fit 5/10 is appropriate.

### Study 10: Teaching exercise through "feel it" cues beats instruction by demonstration on fitness and movement quality
**PMID:** 42804848 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Analyzed sample was 61, not 63** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "63 female university students aged 18–25 were randomized to 32 sessions over 16 weeks"
- **Abstract says:** "63 volunteer female university students aged 18-25 years were randomly assigned... Two participants from the embodied cognition-based group were unable to attend the post-test assessment and were excluded from the final analyses; therefore, the final sample comprised 61 participants."
- **Problem:** The randomized N is right, but the results rest on 61. Worth stating, since two dropouts from a 32-person arm is a non-trivial share.
- **Suggested fix:** "63 female university students aged 18–25 were randomized... with 61 completing post-testing."

**Issue B. Characterization of the two instruction styles** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "does it matter whether the instructor says 'watch me' or 'notice what your ankle is doing'?" / headline "'feel it' cues beats instruction by demonstration"
- **Abstract says:** "traditional instruction and embodied cognition-based training... By emphasizing exploratory learning and sensorimotor awareness..."
- **Problem:** The abstract never describes the verbal cues or says the traditional condition worked by demonstration. The digest's caveat ("loosely defined intervention") and the instruction to "press on how the instruction scripts actually differed" partly cover this, but the headline states the contrast as established fact.
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "Training built on body awareness beats conventional aerobics instruction on fitness and movement quality" — and keep the query about the scripts in the angle.

The fitness outcomes, direction of effect, kinematic findings (reduced knee flexion, greater ankle range of motion) and Kharazmi University authors are correctly reported. NS fit 5/10 is appropriate.

### Study 11: Prescribing exercise for pleasure gets people back to the gym — but not via the motivations theory predicts
**PMID:** 42772728 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N (46), mean age (32), the three-session two-week design, the FITT vs FITT + AFFECT contrast, the absence of significant group-by-time interactions, and the authors' own inference that the parent trial's frequency gain "may operate through mechanisms beyond these constructs" are all represented correctly. The framing is appropriately cautious, the caveats explicitly note that nulls from an underpowered design do not rule out real effects, and the headline correctly attributes the behavioral gain to the parent trial rather than to this analysis. NS fit of 4/10 is, if anything, conservative.

### Study 12: Team sport, solo spinning or karate — the mood lift after exercise looks much the same
**PMID:** 42801814 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Physiological arousal" was self-reported arousal** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the pleasant feeling outlasts the physiological arousal by at least an hour"
- **Abstract says:** "One hour post-exercise, arousal fell below baseline, and positive and negative affect returned to baseline, whereas feeling state remained elevated."
- **Problem:** Arousal here is a self-reported affective dimension, not a physiological measurement — no heart rate or other physiological index is reported in the abstract. The caveats correctly say "self-reported affect," so the body text contradicts the caveat.
- **Suggested fix:** "the pleasant feeling outlasts the sense of arousal by at least an hour"

The N (60), the three sport categories and their interactive/coactive/hybrid labels, the time course, the absence of sport-group effects, the large-effects-only sensitivity and the failure of equivalence tests across all 24 contrasts are all accurately rendered — and the digest deserves credit for refusing to sell the null as equivalence. NS fit 4/10 is appropriate.

### Study 13: Confidence in runners builds in one direction: believing in yourself shapes what you think others think of you
**PMID:** 42722364 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. The reverse path is not explicitly reported as null** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The reverse path did not hold"
- **Abstract says:** "Results revealed a significant cross-lagged effect from self-efficacy at Time 1 to RISE at Time 2, with an indirect effect from self-efficacy at Time 1 to RISE at Time 3 via RISE at Time 2... Findings provide the first longitudinal evidence that self-efficacy may shape RISE beliefs over time, offering new insights into the bidirectional nature of efficacy development."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports only which paths were significant; it does not state that the RISE → self-efficacy path was tested and non-significant (and it oddly refers to "the bidirectional nature of efficacy development"). The inference is probably right but is not confirmable from the abstract.
- **Suggested fix:** "Only the self-efficacy → RISE direction reached significance in the reported results."

N (350), three time points over two months, the RI-CLPM design and its description, the social-identity null and the within-time correlations, and both named authors' affiliations are all accurate. The "first longitudinal evidence" claim matches the abstract. NS fit 4/10 is appropriate.

### Study 14: Most people with hard-to-treat epilepsy or dissociative seizures do no exercise at all
**PMID:** 42700754 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

**Issue A. "Most... do no exercise at all" is not supported** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Most people with hard-to-treat epilepsy or dissociative seizures do no exercise at all"
- **Abstract says:** "PA was low, especially at work (60.0% without PA) and during leisure-time (41.3% without PA). PWE reported less exercise than those with FDS (no exercise: 57.2% vs. 42.6%, p = 0.038)."
- **Problem:** "No exercise" was reported by 57.2% of the epilepsy group but only 42.6% of the FDS group — so "most" is wrong for one of the two groups named in the headline, and marginal across the pooled sample (~52%). The 60% figure is absence of physical activity *at work*, a different measure. The headline merges two incompatible statistics.
- **Suggested fix:** "Around half of people with hard-to-treat epilepsy or dissociative seizures report no exercise at all"

**Issue B. Mechanism speculation presented as the hook** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the within-group difference hints that fear of seizures, not physical incapacity, may be doing the work" / "suggesting the barrier is as much perceived risk and medical caution as pathology."
- **Abstract says:** Nothing about barriers, fear of seizures, or medical advice; the study measured activity levels and instrument psychometrics only.
- **Problem:** The explanation is invented by the digest. It is hedged, but it is also the stated hook of the pitch, which puts the weight of the story on an interpretation the data do not address.
- **Suggested fix:** "the between-group difference raises the question of what drives the gap — the study did not measure barriers, so this is one for the authors."

**Issue C. Unverified background claim about exercise and seizure control** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Exercise is one of the few interventions with evidence across both seizure control and the depression that so often accompanies it"
- **Abstract says:** "This highlights the need for interventions to increase PA in these patient groups." No efficacy evidence is cited.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only; needs an independent source before it runs as a premise.
- **Suggested fix:** Attribute to a cited review or drop.

N (240), the 146/94 split, 86.6% not seizure-free, 65.4% psychiatric comorbidity ("two-thirds"), the 60%/41% activity figures, the 57.2% vs 42.6% direction and the ICC range 0.54–0.75 are all reported correctly. NS fit 4/10 is appropriate.
